scenes.title: Why are big brands invisible to AI?
scenes.sub: Household names keep disappearing from AI answers
scenes.say: Nespresso, Armani, Philips. Everyone knows these brands. But when you ask AI for a coffee machine, a perfume or a robot vacuum, do they get recommended? We measured it. ChatGPT recommended Nespresso in zero of sixteen coffee machine answers. Armani was recommended in none of thirty-two live-search perfume answers. Philips scored zero out of twenty-four on robot vacuums. In this video we look at four patterns in the data, the possible reasons, and how to see this for your own brand.

scenes.title: How we measured

boxes.d: 8 questions per category; no brand names in the questions.
ChatGPT and Claude searched the web; Gemini answered from memory.
The same categories, asked separately in Turkish and English.
How many answers recommended each brand, counted per AI.

scenes.say: Here's the method. In categories like coffee machines, perfume, TVs, robot vacuums, gaming laptops and phones, we asked eight real buyer questions each, with no brand names. ChatGPT and Claude answered with live web search; Gemini answered without search, from memory. We now measure Perplexity too, but it wasn't part of these category runs. Then we counted how many answers recommended each brand, separately for each AI.

scenes.title: Well known, rarely recommended
scenes.note: Live search: ChatGPT + Claude. Gemini sample is small (16 answers).
scenes.say: First, the table. Nespresso was recommended in only three of thirty-one live-search answers, while Gemini, answering from memory, recommended it in thirteen of sixteen. Tom Ford is similar: three with live search, ten on Gemini. In Turkey, Adidas got nine of thirty-two live-search answers, and fifteen of sixteen on Gemini. Armani in perfume and Philips in TVs were never recommended with live search. The Gemini sample is small, so read these gaps as a signal, not a rule.

scenes.title: Fame lives in memory, not in current reviews
scenes.note: Our reading: memory may reflect past fame, live search reflects today's review sites.
scenes.say: Pattern one: an AI answering from memory and an AI searching live don't recommend the same brands. Gemini recommended Nespresso in thirteen of sixteen answers; Claude in three of fifteen; ChatGPT never. Our reading: memory may recall brands people have talked about for years, while live search reads what today's review sites say. So past fame doesn't automatically turn into recommendations from a live-search AI.

scenes.title: The category specialist wins
scenes.note: Observation: for "best X" questions, brands known as specialists were picked.
scenes.say: Pattern two: brands that make everything are absent in some categories. For robot vacuums, Roborock was recommended in twenty-two of twenty-four answers; Philips in none. For coffee machines, De'Longhi nineteen, Siemens zero. For gaming laptops, Lenovo nineteen, Dell three. The data shows that for questions like best robot vacuum, brands known as specialists get picked. A possible reason is that review sites put those brands first too.

scenes.title: One AI recommends it, another never does
scenes.note: Small samples. Possible explanation: ChatGPT gave shorter lists.
scenes.say: Pattern three: one AI recommends a brand, another never does. On US phone questions, Claude recommended Xiaomi in thirteen of twenty-four answers; ChatGPT in none of thirty-two. For MSI gaming laptops, Claude eight, ChatGPT zero. In Turkey, Claude recommended Liv Hospital seven times, ChatGPT never. The samples are small, but they show why measuring your brand on a single AI can mislead.

scenes.title: Local brands are weak even at home
scenes.sub: Turkish questions, live search from Turkey · recommendations
scenes.note: Our reading: being on the review sites AI reads may matter.
scenes.say: Pattern four is about local brands. On coffee machine questions asked in Turkish, from Turkey, Philips was recommended in twenty-three of twenty-nine answers; the Turkish brand Arzum five, Fakir zero. For TVs, Samsung seventeen, and the Turkish brand Vestel just once. A possible reason: a local brand that isn't on the review sites AI reads can be left out even in its home market.

scenes.note: Based on 4 answers (ChatGPT 2, Claude 2; live search, Nov 14, 2026). This is evidence, not a proven cause. Real measurement; brands shown as letters.
scenes.say: So how do you see this for your own brand? This chapter's feature: the Loss Reason Card. For every question where your brand was never recommended but at least one competitor was, AI SaaSavran builds this card. A real example: a major sneaker brand in Turkey; let's call it Brand X. Asked which sneaker brand is the highest quality and longest lasting, Brand X didn't appear once in four live-search answers from ChatGPT and Claude. First, the card shows who was recommended instead: three competitors, each in three of four answers. Then the evidence: the brand's own site was never cited; the answers relied on third-party sites, and the review site RunRepeat was a source in all four. The card doesn't claim a proven cause; it shows the evidence, and tells you where to start. It works on live-search measurements from ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity, and Gemini is measured from memory alongside.

scenes.title: Big brand or not: four steps

boxes.d: Not general awareness: whether you're recommended for each question customers ask.
You can be zero on ChatGPT and strong on Claude.

boxes.t: 3. Check the evidence where you lose
boxes.d: Who was recommended instead, based on which sources?
Be on your category's review sites with accurate, current information.

scenes.say: What should you do? Four steps. One: look at question-by-question results, not general awareness. Two: measure each AI separately; you can be zero on one and strong on another. Three: check the evidence where you lose; who was recommended instead, and based on which sources? Four: be on your category's current review sites with accurate information. Competitor comparison, product accuracy checks and improvement tracking help with these steps too.
